basis: Migne prints his own reference to Genesis 25:1 inside this answer, which asks 'Inter. 218. Cur Abraham post promissum sibi et natum Isaac, in quo ei multiplicatio'. The extent is that reference and nothing wider.
date_basis: The dedicatory letter addresses Sigewulf, Alcuin's pupil and his successor at Tours, and says the questions are ones Sigewulf had put to him over a long acquaintance and are now gathered. Alcuin was abbot of Tours from 796 until his death in 804. The work is conventionally placed in the Tours years and near their beginning; the range records that and no more. The date is the writing, not Migne's 1851 printing, and it is not the seventh century the wiki header gives, which is a century out.
text: Inter. 218. Cur Abraham post promissum sibi et natum Isaac, in quo ei multiplicatio prolis, et benedictio gentium promissa est a Deo, aliam voluit ducere uxorem (Gen. XXV, 1)?-- Resp. Non propter incontinentiam, cum jam esset grandaevus; sed sicut Agar et Ismael significant carnales Veteris Testamenti; sic Cethura et filii ejus significant haereticos, qui se ad Novum Testamentum pertinere existimant. Sed utraeque concubinae dicuntur; sic enim dicitur: Filiis [autem] concubinarum largitus est munera (vers. 6). Sola Sarra uxor semper vocatur.
